Profuse means existing, flowing, or being produced in very large — often overwhelming — amounts. When something is profuse, there is so much of it that it almost seems to pour out or overflow. Think of it as abundance cranked up to a high level.

The simple test: if something is happening or being given in amounts that feel noticeably large, generous, or even excessive, "profuse" is the right word for it.
The Inner Feeling of the Word

The word carries a sense of things flowing freely and generously — almost without restraint. Whether it's blood flowing from a wound, sweat pouring from the body, words of thanks tumbling out of someone's mouth, or flowers blooming everywhere on a plant — when any of these happen in striking, hard-to-ignore quantities, they can be called profuse.

It is not a mild word. You would not use "profuse" to describe a moderate or ordinary amount. It signals something noticeably large.
What Can Be Described as Profuse?

"Profuse" is used with things that can come in varying amounts — things that can be produced, given, emitted, or expressed. Here are the most common real-world uses:

1. Physical bodily things

  • Profuse sweating — sweating heavily, soaking through your clothes.
  • Profuse bleeding — losing a large amount of blood, not just a small cut.
  • Profuse vomiting — vomiting repeatedly and in large amounts.

These are the most medically common uses of the word. Doctors and nurses use it often.

2. Expressions of feelings or words

  • Profuse apologies — apologising over and over again, with a great deal of emotion or words. "He offered profuse apologies for being late."
  • Profuse thanks / gratitude — thanking someone so much that it feels almost excessive. "She was profuse in her thanks."
  • Profuse praise — complimenting someone in large, generous amounts.

3. Nature and growth

  • Profuse vegetation — a thick, lush, dense mass of plants.
  • Profuse blooming — a plant covered in flowers, producing them in great numbers.
  • Profuse rainfall — heavy, abundant rainfall.

4. Other things

  • Profuse notes — writing down a very large number of notes.
  • Profuse tears — crying a lot.

This is where "profuse" gets slightly more interesting. Depending on the context, it can mean either of two things:

Neutral or positive sense (simply "a great deal"):

"The garden was filled with profuse blooms after the monsoon."

Here, it just means there were a lot of flowers. It's a good thing. No negative judgment.

Slightly excessive or overwhelming sense:

"He apologised so profusely that it became uncomfortable."

Here, there's a hint that the amount is more than what was needed — it borders on overdoing it. This is a common subtle undertone with "profuse" when applied to human behaviour (apologies, thanks, praise, tears). It doesn't always mean the person is being fake, but it signals the sheer volume is striking.

Bottom line: "Profuse" can be neutral (just describing a lot) or carry a slight sense of excess (more than expected or needed). Context tells you which one it is.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Since you may encounter these words alongside "profuse," here's how to tell them apart:

  • Abundant — simply "a lot of something," with a positive, natural feel. "Abundant sunshine." It doesn't carry the sense of overflow or excess that "profuse" does.
  • Copious — a large quantity, often used for things you measure or collect: "copious notes," "copious amounts of food." It's more neutral and matter-of-fact than "profuse."
  • Excessive — clearly too much, with a negative judgment built in. "Excessive drinking." It always implies you've crossed a line.
  • Lavish — generous and rich, often applied to spending, decoration, or food. "A lavish dinner." It has a positive or luxurious feeling.
  • Profuse — large amounts, often with a sense of things flowing or pouring out, and sometimes (not always) suggesting the amount is striking or a bit much.

The adverb form of "profuse" is profusely, and it is extremely common in everyday English — perhaps even more common than the adjective itself. It means "in profuse amounts; very abundantly."

  • "She thanked him profusely." (She thanked him a great deal, over and over.)
  • "He was sweating profusely." (He was sweating heavily.)
  • "They apologised profusely." (They apologised many times with great feeling.)
  • "Blood flowed profusely from the wound." (A lot of blood was flowing.)

Whenever you see or hear "profusely," just replace it mentally with "in very large or generous amounts" and you'll understand it perfectly.

"Profuse" is not used for things that don't vary in quantity in a meaningful way, or for abstract concepts. You would not say:

  • ❌ "A profuse idea" (ideas aren't measured in flowing quantities)
  • ❌ "A profuse building"
  • ❌ "A profuse mistake"

It works best when what you're describing is something that can increase or decrease in volume — like liquid, words, growth, emotion, or physical output from the body.

ToneNeutral to slightly excessive; never mild
Used forBodily fluids, emotional expressions (apologies, thanks), natural growth, words, tears

  2. "She received profuse praise from her professor for the quality of her work."
